extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, publicists, and communicators who email journalists with press releases/pitches
extracted.subtask_description: Data-driven guidance for writing subject lines for press release / journalist outreach emails, focused on maximizing opens, replies, and click-throughs while avoiding spam filters and mobile truncation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line length / mobile truncation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 10 words / 50 characters for highest open rates; cut off on mobile after 60 characters; most journalists first see emails on mobile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep subject lines short (≤50 characters / <10 words) so the key message isn't truncated on mobile (mobile cutoff ~60 characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization (mention publication/journalist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization: 50.81% open rate when mentioning publication vs 39.25% without mention — a +11.56 percentage-point lift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention the publication or recipient (e.g., 'For [Publication]') to materially increase open rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual formatting — use brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject lines with brackets achieved a 52.08% open rate and a 2.24% reply rate; noted as the best performing format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adding brackets (e.g., [Exclusive], [Data], [Study]) to improve visibility and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question / curiosity-inducing format
rubrics_metrics.description: Question format performs well (example: 'How Did This Startup Increase Revenue 300%?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a curiosity-driven question or specific claim to entice opens without being vague or clickbaity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Exclusive' / offer exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive offers (e.g., 'Exclusive: [Story]') produce significant open-rate lifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with exclusivity when applicable to signal value to the journalist (e.g., exclusive access, embargoed data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include specific numbers / measurable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject lines with numbers and specific outcomes (e.g., '[Number] + [Specific outcome]') perform strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete metrics or results in the subject line to signal newsworthiness and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject lines that include a local city or regional angle (e.g., '[Local city] + [news]') perform well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story has local relevance, surface the city/region in the subject line to target appropriate reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity / notable-person reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing a notable person or celebrity in the subject line can increase open rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name recognizable people when they are legitimately part of the news (e.g., '[Notable person] joins [Company]').

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-performing formats to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Formats that underperform include: 'Press Release: [topic]', 'For Your Consideration', 'Just Following Up', ALL CAPS, multiple exclamation points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic, formulaic, or aggressive formats that read like mass blasts or follow-ups; don't use all caps or excessive punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize click-through / story delivery (not just opens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open rate ≠ click-through rate (CTR). 'PR' in the subject line may give a slight open bump but provides no CTR lift. CTR is the more important metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write subject lines and ensure the email body (headline + summary) actually delivers the promised value so recipients click; subject lines should set up a headline/summary that converts to CTR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spam-filter triggers to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases and signals that can trigger spam filters include: 'Limited time', 'Must-see', 'Free', '$$$', ALL CAPS, excessive punctuation, 'Click here', 'Act now'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these words/formatting and excessive punctuation; keep language natural and journalistic to reduce spam risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the news angle clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject line should show the news angle clearly (what's newsworthy about the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the news hook explicit (e.g., new data, an event, a notable hire) so journalists can quickly assess relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer something of value
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality subject lines communicate an offer — exclusive access, data, or expert sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal what you're offering (exclusive interview, unique dataset, expert comment) rather than a bland announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject lines should be free of jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain, specific language a journalist would understand immediately; remove internal jargon or marketing fluff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read-aloud / recipient-priority test
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit quality test: Read aloud. Would a journalist with 200 unread emails open this one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a final check, read the subject line aloud and judge whether it would cut through a crowded inbox — if not, revise.
